articles.summary: You're halfway through mowing your lawn when your phone goes off in your pocket. You lift one earmuff to answer the call, mower still running beside you. That same ear stays uncovered for the length of the call, taking all the noise damage from the mower without you even noticing. Bluetooth hearing protection is built for that scenario. Your earmuffs, earbuds, or earplugs rely on a seal around your ear to protect your hearing. Any time that seal is disrupted, your hearing protection gear fails. Bluetooth hearing protection holds that seal while a phone call comes through the same speakers that handle your hearing enhancement. A shooting range, a job site, and yard each ask something different from your hearing protection gear. Where you spend your time Hearing protection gear that best fits Why Indoor range Bluetooth earmuffs Highest ratings, and no insertion technique to get wrong Outdoor range, rifles, and shotguns Bluetooth earbuds Nothing between your cheek and your rifle stock Full days on a job site Bluetooth earmuffs 30 to 40 hour runtimes, easy to take on and off between tasks Working under a hard hat Bluetooth earbuds Your headwear never touches the seal Mowing, sawing, and yard work Bluetooth earbuds Rated against sweat and rain, stays comfortable for hours A spare pair for your truck Passive earplugs Cheap, and has no battery that needs charging What Bluetooth Adds to Hearing Protection, and What It Costs Bluetooth does not weaken your hearing protection. The wireless audio path and the compression circuit are separate systems, and neither involves wireless audio. Your ear cushion or ear tip provides the physical seal that protects your hearing. A compression circuit clamps a loud sound before your speakers pass it along your ear, and AXIL sets that circuit at 85 dB across the electronic line. Bluetooth Adds Calls, Streaming and a Reason to Keep Your Protection On A Bluetooth feature in your hearing protection gear lets you take a call without lifting an earmuff off your ear. You would be able to stream music and podcasts through the same speakers carrying your hearing enhancement, so your protection stays sealed through a four hour job or a two hour shooting range session. Some models hold a link to a second device, which keeps your phone and your truck stereo connected at the same time. That gives you the benefit of not having to take your hearing protection off. Hearing protection only works while a pair is on your head. Every reason to pull off your gear is a moment when your ears are at risk. Bluetooth Costs You a Battery and a Charging Habit A wireless audio path needs power, which means a battery in your earmuffs or your earbuds and a charger to plug them into. AXIL carries the CRX LINK adaptor that adds Bluetooth to its CRX earbuds at a slightly higher price point than just the base earbuds. One thing to check before buying Bluetooth hearing protection is what happens to your gear when the battery dies out. On most electronic hearing protection, the ear cushion or ear tip still seals your ears even when it’s out of juice. You’ll keep your passive protection but lose your electronic hearing enhancement. Some models handle a dead battery differently, so check that behavior on the product page before you buy. Tip: If charging your gear is the part you would often forget, look for a Bluetooth earmuff that runs on replaceable batteries. The SIG SAUER TRACKR BLU takes two AAA cells, so you can carry spares in your range bag. You can learn more about compression circuits and reaction speed on our guide to how electronic hearing protection works. The Bluetooth feature itself matters less than the form factor carrying it. Bluetooth Earmuffs vs Earbuds vs Earplugs Bluetooth earmuffs, Bluetooth earbuds, and passive earplugs all seal your ears. How each gear gets the seal right decides which of the three belongs in your bag. Bluetooth earmuffs Bluetooth earbuds Passive earplugs Typical AXIL rating 22 dB NRR to 30 dB SNR 17 to 23 dB NRR 13 to 19 dB NRR Runtime, audio plus enhancement 30 to 40 hours 5 to 15 hours No battery Getting a consistent seal Put them on and you're sealed You have to choose the right tip size for your ear and practice on how to get the seal right You have to choose the right tip size for your ear and practice on how to get the seal right Rifle cheek weld Cup can catch your stock Nothing in the way Nothing in the way Under a hard hat or a beanie Headband fights your headwear Unaffected Unaffected Heat and sweat Cups hold heat on long days Small contact area Small contact area AXIL price band $138.99 to $153.99 $123.06 to $307.67 $38.99 Bluetooth Earmuffs Give You the Same Seal Every Time An earmuff seals against the side of your head, so you just put a pair on and you get close to the rated protection. That’s it, you’re all set. That ease of putting your hearing protection gear on and off suits a range regular, and anyone handing a pair to a guest shooter. Bigger gear housings also fit bigger batteries, so a Bluetooth earmuff can run 30 hours of music and hearing enhancement together. The trade off is contact. Earmuff cups can hold heat on a summer afternoon, a headband fights your hard hat, and the edge of a cup can catch your rifle stock. Bluetooth Earbuds Stay Clear of Your Rifle and Your Hard Hat A Bluetooth earbud seals inside your ear canal, which leaves the outside of your head free. Nothing sits between your cheek and your rifle stock, your hard hat goes on normally, and a long afternoon doesn't turn into sweat under a foam cushion. The tradeoff here is technique. A Bluetooth earbud only delivers its protection rating once you've sized the ear tip and seated it past the bend in your ear canal. Battery runtimes come down too, since a battery small enough to sit in your ear holds less charge. Passive Earplugs Are Cheap and Easy to Carry Everywhere Passive earplugs win a narrower argument. A pair with no battery can live in your truck, your range bag, and your mower shed easily. What you give up is the hearing enhancement feature and bluetooth audio, but you’ll get protection that's never out of charge. Form factor decides which pair you can wear all day. The next thing to figure out is what type of hearing protection rating you need depending on your activity. How Much Protection Do You Need for Your Environment? A chainsaw, a push mower, and an indoor range are different problems, and one protection rating can’t serve all three. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) puts its recommended exposure limit at 85 A-weighted decibels across an eight hour day, and cuts the safe duration in half for every 3 dBA above that. Nine decibels of extra noise turns an eight hour allowance into one hour. NIOSH measurements of landscaping equipment put a push mower at 86 to 92 dBA, a leaf blower at 95 to 106 dBA, and a chainsaw at 105 to 109 dBA. A push mower asks for a few decibels of reduction. A chainsaw asks for more than twenty, across every minute the saw runs. Gunfire belongs in a separate category because that noise arrives inside a millisecond instead of across an hour. NIOSH reports gunfire often reaching 160 to 170 dB peak sound pressure. Indoor ranges push higher again, and NIOSH recommends doubling up with earplugs under earmuffs for that kind of impulse noise. The doubling-up recommendation is why a landscaper and a range regular can land on different gear. A landscaper needs a rating that holds across eight hours. A range regular needs the rating plus a second layer for a few dozen loud instants. Your Seal Decides How Much of That Rating You Get NIOSH states that laboratory-based hearing protector ratings overestimate the protection workers get in the field. A well-seated 22 dB pair can beat a badly seated 30 dB pair. Our guide to Noise Reduction Ratings discusses how those numbers are measured, and our decibel guide lists levels for more environments. A rating matched to your environment is the first thing to check on a spec sheet. Six other specs decide whether a pair holds up for your daily use. What to Check Before You Buy Bluetooth Hearing Protection When you know what environment you’ll be working in and what target rating you need from your hearing protection, six other specs decide whether a Bluetooth pair actually works for you: Protection rating matched to your environment, in Noise Reduction Rating (NRR) or Single Number Rating (SNR), with the ear tip or cushion you'll use Runtime against your real session length, plus what your pair does when the battery reaches zero Pairing capability, including whether your gear can pair with two devices at once Microphone quality, if you take calls in a noisy environment Controls you can work with gloves or a shooting glove on Water and sweat resistance, with a published IP rating instead of a general claim Compatibility with the hard hat, helmet, or hat you often wear Protection rating sits at the top because a lower number than what your environment demands won’t give you the hearing protection you need. Pairing behavior is easy to skip past on a spec sheet. AXIL's MX PRO earmuffs run Bluetooth 5.4 and connect to one device at a time, so moving from your truck stereo to your phone means a manual reconnect. If you switch devices several times a day, look for multipoint by name. Radio capability is also worth checking separately. Most current Bluetooth hearing protection streams from your phone instead of carrying an AM/FM tuner. If you want a radio built into your earmuffs, confirm the tuner on the spec sheet before you order. Match the List to How You'll Use Your Gear Where you spend your time Start with Because At an indoor range Bluetooth earmuffs Consistent seal for you and for anyone you hand a pair to On a job site all day Bluetooth earmuffs Runtime clears a full day with audio running Behind a rifle or in a stand Bluetooth earbuds Cheek weld and headwear stay normal In the yard on weekends Bluetooth earbuds with an IP65 rating Sweat, rain and long sessions without cup pressure Across all three Bluetooth earbuds and a spare set of earplugs One pair that travels, one pair that never needs charging AXIL's Bluetooth line divides along those same seven specs, mostly on rating, runtime and fit hardware. AXIL Bluetooth Earmuffs, Earbuds and Earplugs, Matched to Your Activity AXIL splits its Bluetooth line across the same three form factors, and each one has an obvious home. AXIL Bluetooth Earmuffs for the Range and the Job Site The MX PRO carries a 30 dB Single Number Rating and runs 30 hours with hearing enhancement and audio together. The MXII PRO carries a 22 dB NRR, an IP65 rating, and a compartment in the cup that stores a pair of AXIL earplugs for doubling up at an indoor range. Best for: indoor ranges and full days on a job site. The SIG SAUER TRACKR BLU is the slimline earmuff option if you want the co-brand. A 27 dB SNR and a 0.02 second compression reaction time run on two AAA batteries, so you carry spare cells instead of planning around a charger. Best for: range days where charging is the part you'd forget. AXIL Bluetooth Earbuds for Shooting, Work and the Yard The GS Extreme 3.0 is the all-round Bluetooth earbud. Foam tips carry a 21 dB NRR, an Ingress Protection (IP) 65 rating handles rain and sweat, and 15 hours of combined use covers a full day outdoors. The concha locks hold the fit no matter how you move. Best for: long days outside across shooting, work and yard equipment. The XCOR PRO is the flagship in-ear gear, at a 21 to 23 dB NRR with foam tips, and six times amplification. Bluetooth audio and hearing enhancement run about five hours, which trades runtime for cheek weld and all-day comfort. Best for: rifle shooters and hunters who need their stock to sit clean. The CRX is the entry point into electronic protection at $123.06, with a 20 dB NRR on foam tips, and 10 hours of battery runtime. Bluetooth is not built in, so a CRX pair needs the CRX LINK adaptor before it will stream. Best for: a first electronic pair for weekend saw and mower work. AXIL Earplugs for the Pair That Lives in Your Truck The X30i is the passive counterpoint for in-ear protection. A toggle valve on each earplug moves you between 19 dB NRR closed and 16 dB NRR open, with no battery involved. The same earplugs fit inside the MXII PRO cup, which makes them a good second layer for an indoor range session. Best for: a spare pair for your truck, or anyone who decides electronics aren't worth it. Bluetooth Ear Protection FAQs Do Bluetooth ear muffs protect your hearing? Yes, to whatever NRR or SNR the model carries. Your seal and your compression circuit do that work, and the Bluetooth audio path runs separately from both. Is Bluetooth hearing protection OSHA approved? OSHA rates the hearing protector, not the Bluetooth. Your rating and your fit are what the standard addresses, and some sites ban listening devices regardless of rating. Can you listen to music and still hear a gunshot safely? Yes. The compression circuit clamps the impulse at the microphone before your speakers pass it along, whether or not music is playing. What happens when the battery dies? Your ear cushion or ear tip keeps sealing on most models, so you hold your passive protection and lose hearing enhancement. Confirm the behavior on the product page before you buy. What NRR do I need for mowing, shooting or a job site? Around 20 to 25 dB NRR, well sealed, covers most outdoor shooting and yard equipment. If you're shooting indoors or running a chainsaw all day, consider earplugs under earmuffs. Getting Your First Bluetooth Hearing Protection Right Buy for the environment you're in most often instead of the one you just visit occasionally. A shooter who spends 40 weekends a year at an indoor range and two weekends in a deer stand should buy earmuffs for the range and borrow hearing protection for the stand. A full-time carpenter who spends a few weekends mowing their lawn should get hearing protection for the job site instead of the yard. Once you have your gear in hand, give it a first session test to get the seal right. Put your pair on with the electronics off and talk out loud. Your own voice should sound boomy and muffled inside your head. If your voice sounds close to normal, air is leaking past your ear tip or your cushion, and the rating on the box is not reaching your eardrum. Go up a size in your ear tips and seat them again, or reposition your headband until your voice changes. A good seal pays off more than any other gear spec. Your hearing enhancement sounds cleaner with less outside noise competing against it, your music sits at a lower volume, and your protection holds for the length of the day. A Bluetooth pair that seals properly gives you your protection, your conversation, and your audio at the same time, without you taking the gear off. Shop AXIL Bluetooth hearing protection across earmuffs, earbuds and earplugs, and match your first pair to the noise you stand in most.

articles.summary: 10-year financing to support ReNew’s under-construction renewable energy portfolio and deepen access to long-term international capital Gurugram, India; October 13, 2026: ReNew (“ ReNew ” or “the Company”), one of India’s leading decarbonisation solutions companies, today announced that it has secured a USD 100 million (approximately INR 955 crore) financing facility from FMO (Nederlandse Financierings -Maatschappij voor Ontwikkelingslanden N.V.), the Dutch entrepreneurial development bank. Extended to ReNew Solar Power Private Limited under the Voluntary Retention Route (VRR), the 10-year financing will support renewable energy projects currently under construction across the ReNew group. The transaction marks FMO’s largest single-ticket investment in India’s energy sector and its largest 2X-aligned corporate financing in Asia to date, underscoring the growing role of international development finance in supporting India’s clean energy transition. The facility qualifies under the 2X Challenge, a global initiative focused on advancing women’s economic participation and empowerment through investment. Proceeds from the INR-denominated financing will be deployed towards ReNew’s under-construction renewable energy projects. The long-term financing strengthens ReNew’s access to international capital and further diversifies its funding base across domestic and global markets. With a 10-year tenor aligned with the long operating life of renewable energy assets, the facility provides stable capital to support the Company’s expanding portfolio and continued growth. Kailash Vaswani, Chief Financial Officer, ReNew , said: “This financing is a strong endorsement of ReNew’s scale, execution capabilities and long-term growth strategy, and reflects the confidence of leading global institutions in India’s clean energy opportunity. The 10-year facility gives us access to stable, long-term capital at a critical stage of our portfolio build-out, while further diversifying our funding sources across international and domestic markets. We are delighted to strengthen our partnership with FMO and channel this capital towards projects that will contribute to India’s rapidly expanding clean energy ecosystem.” Marnix Monsfort , Director & Head – Energy, FMO, said: “We are pleased to partner with ReNew on this 2X-aligned investment and support the Company’s growth ambitions. As FMO’s largest investment in India’s energy sector, this transaction demonstrates our commitment to supporting India’s energy transition through impactful, large-scale financing solutions. ReNew has established itself as a leading renewable energy company in the country, and we look forward to supporting its continued contribution to India’s clean energy future.” The financing comes at a pivotal moment in India’s energy transition, as the country accelerates the deployment of renewable energy and the investment required to build the infrastructure of a low-carbon economy. For ReNew , the transaction reinforces its ability to mobilise long-term global capital at scale and deploy it towards projects that expand India’s clean energy capacity. It also deepens the Company’s relationship with FMO and reflects a shared commitment to financing an energy transition that is sustainable, inclusive and economically resilient. About ReNew ReNew is a leading decarbonization solutions company listed on Nasdaq (Nasdaq: RNW, RNWWW). ReNew’s clean energy portfolio of 20.5 GW (including 1.7 GW/6.2 GWh of BESS) on a gross basis as of August 18, 2026, is one of the largest globally. In addition to being a major independent power producer in India, we provide end-to-end solutions in a just and inclusive manner in the areas of clean energy, value-added energy offerings through digitalization, storage, and carbon markets that are increasingly integral to addressing climate change. In addition, ReNew has 6.4 GW of solar module and 2.5 GW of solar cell manufacturing capacities and is expanding its solar cells manufacturing capacity by another 4 GW, which is expected to be operational by December 2026. For more information, visit www.renew.com and follow us on LinkedIn, Facebook, X, and Instagram. Media enquiries: pr@renew.com About FMO FMO is the Dutch entrepreneurial development bank. As a leading impact investor, FMO supports sustainable private sector growth in developing countries and emerging markets by investing in ambitious projects and entrepreneurs. FMO believes that a strong private sector leads to economic and social development and has a 50+ year proven track-record in empowering entrepreneurs to make local economies more inclusive, productive, resilient and sustainable. FMO focuses on three sectors that have high development impact: Agribusiness, Food & Water, Energy, and Financial Institutions. With a total committed portfolio of EUR ~13 billion spanning over 85 countries, FMO is one of the larger bilateral private sector development banks globally. For more information: please visit www.fmo.nl Policy Declaration: www.fmo.nl/independent-complaints-mechanism

The project was originally designed to produce 2500t/day of clinker, sufficient for 0.9Mt/yr of cement. The company had later planned to increase its capacity to 6000t/day of clinker (2.2Mt/yr of cement), but failed to secure funding for implementation. The project has faced delays since it was announced in 2013. Authorities in Thanh Hoa repeatedly proposed halting it, and the ministry now says it no longer aligns with the province’s 2021 – 2030 development plan. The project site falls within the safety perimeter of a defence facility. The limestone and clay deposits intended to supply raw materials are also in an area where mineral extraction is prohibited. Local opposition is another major obstacle. Of 717 households surveyed across five nearby villages, 715 opposed the project over concerns about pollution and health impacts.

Originally dedicated in 1950, the bell became a centerpiece of Arizona’s statewide efforts commemorating the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Phelps Dodge Corp. and Miami Copper Co., both later acquired by Freeport, were among the original sponsors that funded the bell in 1950. Arizona’s bell was one of 53 replicas delivered to states and territories as part of a U.S. Savings Bond drive. The bells were modeled after the original Liberty Bell at Independence Hall in Philadelphia.

articles.summary: Coyote hunting can be more punishing on your gear than almost any other hunt in North America. You're usually hunting solo, often cold, and probably sitting in the dark waiting on an animal that can pick out one wrong sound from two hundred yards out. A missed layer, a caller in the wrong spot, or a bad hearing amplifier can end a stand before it starts. This guide walks through the full kit you’ll need to hunt coyotes: rifle, calls, optics, seating gear, and hearing protection. You'll get the lowdown of a complete coyote hunting gear checklist so you can build a kit that fits how you hunt. Building a Coyote Hunting Kit From the Ground Up A coyote hunting kit is built from six categories: firearms and ammunition, calling gear, optics and light, concealment and apparel, seating and stability, and support gear. Here’s a full checklist first for a quick look:. Category Starter Kit Dedicated Night-Hunter Setup Firearm & Ammo Bolt or semi-auto rifle in .223/5.56, factory varmint loads AR platform with a suppressor mount, hand-loaded or match-grade ammunition Calling Mouth call (open reed or howler) Electronic caller with a detached, remote-controlled speaker Optics & Light Variable daytime scope (3-9x or similar), handheld red or green spotlight Thermal monocular for scanning, dedicated night vision or thermal weapon optic, gun-mounted light with adjustable output Concealment & Apparel Insulated camo layers matched to terrain, face covering Same, plus wind-blocking outer shell and heavyweight gloves for long stationary sits Seating & Stability Foldable low-profile hunting stool Swivel seat or ground blind chair, shooting tripod or bipod Support Gear Small daypack, rangefinder, knife Pack built for moving between five or six stands, spare batteries, backup light Hearing protection Passive foam plugs Electronic in-ear hearing protection with amplification and wind filtering Budget Tiers: Starter Kit vs. Dedicated Night-Hunter Setup Coyote hunters often spend heavily on optics and stay frugal everywhere else. A starter kit for running daylight just needs a rifle you already own, a mouth call, and a decent daytime scope. Night hunting can punch your budget up, since thermal and night vision gear carries the highest price tag. If you’re starting out on your journey, add to what you already own instead of buying the full list at once. What Caliber Should You Use for Coyote Hunting? Most coyote hunters do well with something in the .223/5.56 family, and the choice comes down to one tradeoff: velocity versus pelt damage. The Velocity vs. Pelt Damage Tradeoff A fast, light bullet drops a coyote quickly but can wreck a pelt at close range. A heavier, slower round is more pelt-friendly but asks more from your shot placement. Here's how the common coyote calibers stack up. Caliber Typical Effective Range Pelt Damage Best For .223/5.56 Out to 300 yards Moderate, worse at close range with fast varmint loads The default all-around coyote round, especially in an AR platform .22-250 Out to 350+ yards Higher at close range due to velocity Open-country hunters prioritizing flat trajectory over pelt condition .243 Winchester Out to 350 yards Lower with controlled-expansion bullets Crossover big-game hunters who want one rifle for deer and coyotes 6.5 Grendel Out to 300 yards Low to moderate AR shooters who want more downrange energy without giving up the platform .204 Ruger Out to 300 yards Low, known for pelt-friendly performance Fur hunters prioritizing hide condition above all else Is .308 Too Big for Coyote Hunting? This gun works at any range you can hit a coyote, but at typical calling distances, it can be overkill for the animal and hard on the pelt. That’s something you want to keep in mind if you intend to sell its fur. Otherwise, caliber choice comes down to what you already own and shoot well. Why the AR Platform Wins Fast Follow-Ups The AR platform dominates predator hunting because fast follow-up shots count for a lot on a pair or small group. AR-platform rifles also run suppressors and mount optics more easily. Bolt guns still make sense for the hunter who wants one rifle for deer season too. Shot distances in coyote hunting run shorter than most hunters expect. It’s often inside 150 yards, since calling brings the animal to you. That’s what makes the call you choose matter more than the caliber you shoot. Calling Coyotes: Gear, Sounds, and Sequencing Basics Electronic Callers vs. Mouth Calls You’ll need a call to bring a coyote inside your shooting range. An electronic caller with a detached, remote speaker can put the sound away from your position while you stay still. A coyote will walk toward the speaker, not you. Pair this with a motion decoy sitting downwind of your position, so a coming coyote has something to focus on besides you. Mouth calls still earn a place in your kit: they cost far less, don’t need batteries, and let a practiced hunter run realistic sequences by hand. But you’ll be broadcasting the sound from your own position, which is something to keep in mind. Core Sound Categories by Season There are three sound categories that cover most hunting situations: Prey distress (rabbit, fawn) draws hungry coyotes nearly any time. Coyote vocalizations (howls, barks, challenge calls) work best when you want to take advantage of territorial pressure, typically during the breeding season into early spring. Pup distress works in late spring and summer, when adults are protecting a den. Running a Calling Sequence Tip: Start every stand at a lower volume than you think you need. The most common beginner mistake is opening at full volume, which can spook a coyote that's already closer than you realize. A basic sequence starts low. Scan the area while the call plays, and raise the volume only if nothing shows after several minutes. Watching your environment is just as important as calling because coyotes often approach silently. You know how to get a coyote’s attention. But seeing it, especially after dark, is a separate problem with its own gear curve. How to Choose Optics for Coyote Hunting No single optic covers daylight calling and a night-long thermal scan equally well. Choosing the best gear for you is all about matching the right optic to when and how you hunt. Thermal vs. Night Vision: What Each One Solves Thermal and night vision solve two different problems: thermal finds animals by heat, night vision confirms what you found by amplifying available light. Feature Thermal Night Vision How it detects Senses heat signatures against the surrounding background Amplifies existing light (moon, stars, ambient) Best at Finding animals in total darkness, heavy cover, or fog Positive identification and precise shot placement Weak point Struggles to show fine detail for identification Needs some ambient light to perform well Typical role Handheld scanner to locate Weapon-mounted optic, or daytime glass, to confirm and shoot The Scanner-Plus-Scope Workflow Most dedicated night hunters use the same technique: using handheld thermal monocular scans for heat signatures, then a weapon-mounted optic to confirm the target for the shot. One good thermal scanner is all you really need if you already have an adequate rifle scope. Choosing Daytime Glass for Realistic Coyote Distances Most coyote hunting still happens in daylight so you’ll need daytime glass. Calling shots can run short, so a lower-magnification variable scope like in the 3-9x range beats a high-power long-range setup. Detection Range vs. Identification Range The detection range printed on a thermal unit's box is not the same as its real identification range in the field. A unit that claims to detect a coyote-sized target at 1,000 yards might only let you identify it at a fraction of that distance. Instead, double-check the thermal unit’s refresh rate, resolution, and cold-weather battery life before choosing the best gear for you. Choosing the right optic gets your eyes on a coyote. Sitting motionless and staying silent long enough are all part of the hunt, and it's only sustainable if you're comfortable. Staying Steady and Still on a Coyote Stand Seating is one of the most undervalued categories in a coyote hunter's kit. A stand can run twenty to forty minutes long. You’re more likely to move around if you’re sitting uncomfortably. To make sure you don’t end the stand too early, you’ll need a low-profile chair or cushion that keeps you off the cold, uneven ground. Swivel Seats Solve the Direction Problem A coyote rarely commits from the exact direction you're facing when you start the stand. A swivel seat solves that. You can turn toward a sound or movement without standing up, shuffling your feet, or making noise, so you stay ready without giving away your position. Tripods Cover the 360-Degree Problem Tripods and shooting sticks solve that same movement issue, but for your rifle. A rest that covers only one arc leaves you exposed on the other three-quarters of the field. A shooting tripod that pivots smoothly covers a far wider window than a fixed bipod. Packing to Move Between Five or Six Stands If you’re moving between five or six stands, you’ll need a small, purpose-built pack instead of a full backcountry rig. Make sure you’ve got spare batteries, a rangefinder, extra ammunition, and a way to carry the caller and decoy without noise. Less fumbling between stands means less movement once you're set up. In-Ear Protection for Predator Hunters The last piece of gear you need is for your ears, and it’s something most gear guides skip. If you’re sitting in the dark and buffeted by wind, listening for an approach you can’t see, you’ll need electronic hearing amplification. Passive plugs won’t work here because they take away the exact sound you’re waiting for: a stick breaking or a paw landing on frozen ground thirty yards out. At the same time, your rifle blast presents your ears with real risk. Peak sound pressure levels from firearms typically run 140 to 175 decibels, and OSHA treats 140 dB peak as the threshold where impulse noise turns hazardous to unprotected ears. A .223 out of a short AR barrel sits well inside that range, and coyote hunters often shoot from awkward positions with the muzzle close to their own head. Why In-Ear Wins Over Muffs for Predator Hunters In-ear hearing protection units can fit under a beanie or hood without the bulk of the ear muffs. They won’t interfere with cheek weld, and don’t leave cups for the wind to catch and roar into the microphone. Wind filtering is important in a coyote stand, since you're amplifying sound in open country. Best for: The AXIL ear buds collection works for predator hunters who need amplification and wind filtering in a low-profile. For the full breakdown of formats and specs across hunting disciplines, check out our hunting ear protection guide. Quick Answers to Common Coyote Hunting Gear Questions What is the must-have gear for coyote hunting? A rifle you shoot well, a call, wind awareness, a way to sit still, and a way to see in the dark if you hunt nights. Everything else on the checklist above is optimization once those five pieces are covered. What is the best setup for coyote hunting? Wind in your face, sun at your back, an elevated view of the likely approach, and your caller and decoy placed downwind and away from your own position rather than right beside you. Do you need thermal to hunt coyotes? You don't. Daylight calling works without any night optics at all. Thermal is an upgrade that expands when and how much you can hunt, particularly after dark. How long should you stay on a stand? Twenty to forty minutes typically, longer in thick cover or under heavy hunting pressure. The seat and layering covered earlier are what make that possible, not willpower. Your Ears Are the One Piece of Gear You Use on Every Stand A successful coyote hunt depends on your hearing the animal approach. The hunter who can solve the unglamorous problems of seating, wind roar, and hearing beats out any hunter who owns the priciest optic on the field. A starter kit built around your rifle, a mouth call, a comfortable seat, and solid wind awareness puts coyotes in front of you. A dedicated night-hunter setup layers thermal, night vision, and electronic calling on top of that same foundation. Your hearing works for both summer daylight sits and January night hunts. Every other category here changes with caliber, season, or light. Hearing is the one constant. Shop for hunting hearing protection built for hunters who need to hear the approach before they see it.

articles.summary: 10/13/26 Semrush Releases 2026 AI Visibility Index, Revealing Its First UK Benchmark Latest 2026 AI Visibility Index finds that the brands and sources surfaced by AI vary significantly between the UK and US — and that visibility on one AI platform does not guarantee visibility on another. Semrush, an Adobe company and the leading brand visibility platform, today announced the latest edition of its 2026 AI Visibility Index at Spotlight London, expanding its flagship research with a dedicated comparison on how major AI platforms surface brands and sources in the UK and US. The findings show that there is no single, global approach by which AI visibility is achieved. The brands that AI platforms mention, the sources they cite, and the level of consistency between platforms all differ by market. The new report analyzes seven months (January - July 2026) of AI visibility data across fixed monthly sets of 2.5 million UK and 25 million US prompts, built from Semrush search data, across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Google AI Mode, alongside a larger variable dataset of Google AI Overviews results for real search keywords. Across all seven monthly benchmarks, the four AI platforms agreed less in the UK than in the US on which brands to mention and which sources to cite. On average, any two platforms shared 63 to 70 of their top 100 mentioned brands in the UK, compared with 70 to 78 in the US. The study finds that Gemini mentions more distinct brands per answer than ChatGPT, while ChatGPT cites the most sources per answer of the four platforms studied. The result is a more fragmented AI visibility landscape in which brands need to understand their position by market, platform, and category, rather than relying on a single global ranking or approach. A strategy built for US AI answers may not transfer to the UK with the same results, and success requires a tailored, market-specific strategy to address each platform’s source mix and local domain signals like media, publishers, and communities. For enterprise brands, brand and AI visibility is a global concern. And with every additional market comes additional complexity. Brands need to optimize their own content for the audiences, questions, and expectations of each market, while also building the right third-party signals around them. -Marissa Dacay, Global Vice President, Enterprise Marketing, Adobe As the landscape continues to grow increasingly complex, the commercial stakes are also growing. Adobe data cited in the report shows that AI-referred visitors convert 60% better than non-AI traffic and generate 53% more revenue per visit. This underscores AI’s increasing role in consumer discovery, evaluation, and selection. Each Market Has Its Own Always-Visible Brands The Index identifies a persistent group of brands that appear among the top 100 mentions on all four AI platforms in every month measured — described in the study as the Universal Core. Twenty-four UK domain records met that standard, compared with 36 in the US, with only 15 domains shared across both markets, including Adobe, Apple, Amazon, Google, LinkedIn, Microsoft, Reddit, TikTok and YouTube. The UK-specific group is strikingly retail-led. Six of the nine domains unique to the UK Universal Core are ecommerce or retail brands: Amazon UK, Argos, Asda, eBay UK, Marks & Spencer and Tesco. BBC, Nike and TripAdvisor UK complete the UK-specific group. The US-specific set is considerably broader, spanning automotive, sport, entertainment and retail. The findings highlight how local brand ecosystems continue to matter even for global companies. A brand that is consistently visible in one market may have a very different AI footprint in another. AI is now a decision layer for customers, changing how they discover brands, sort through options and ultimately purchase. That makes visibility a business and commercial growth issue, not only a search issue. The sources and brands that shape decisions in the UK are not identical to those in the US, and teams need to build for those differences while keeping brands consistently discovered, evaluated and chosen wherever AI is shaping the decision. -Andrew Warden, Global Vice President of Marketing and CMO of Semrush, An Adobe Company UK AI Answers Rely More Heavily on News One of the clearest differences in the Index is the role that news and information publishers play across the two regions. In the UK, news publishers play a more dominant role in AI answers. On ChatGPT, news sites accounted for an average 29.5% of citations among the 100 most-cited UK domains, against 19.6% in the US. On Gemini, news was the leading UK source category in every month, at between 16.6% and 23.0% of top-100 citations. On ChatGPT, trip-planning sites and online marketplaces follow news in the UK, while online learning and streaming platforms follow it in the US. For brands, the findings reinforce the importance of third-party authority. AI visibility is shaped both by what a company says about itself, and what others say about it: publishers, marketplaces, communities and forums, and other independent sources. Those sources increasingly form part of the information layer AI systems use to answer user questions. Being Mentioned Is Not the Same as Being Cited The report also reinforces a central finding of the previous AI Visibility Index: being mentioned by an AI platform and being cited are two different forms of visibility. Averaged across 22 categories and four platforms, fewer than half of the top 100 mentioned brands also appear among the top 100 cited domains, in every month and in both markets. In the UK, average overlap across the study ranged from just 36.7 to 45.3 domains out of 100, depending on the month. The gap can be substantial even between direct competitors. In the UK, Tesco and Asda both remained among the top 100 mentioned brands across all four platforms in every month studied. Yet in July, Tesco ranked as ChatGPT's 25th most-cited UK domain, while Asda ranked 606th. On Gemini, the same two brands were considerably closer, ranking 29th and 60th respectively for citations. The example demonstrates why marketers cannot treat brand visibility in LLMs as a single score. Additional AI Visibility Index Takeaways Beyond the headline findings, the study reveals several important dynamics shaping how brands appear, compete, and build trust across AI-powered discovery environments: Each platform creates a different visibility environment. Gemini mentions more distinct brands per answer than ChatGPT, while ChatGPT cites the most sources per answer and Gemini the fewest. Google AI Overviews responses are particularly distinct. Across all seven months, brand mention overlap was consistently lowest in Google AI Overviews compared to the other three platforms. Its pairing with ChatGPT also has the lowest source overlap of any two platforms, in both markets. UK visibility is more fragmented across platforms. A larger share of leading UK domains appears on only one AI platform, reinforcing the need to measure ChatGPT, Gemini, AI Mode and AI Overviews independently rather than assuming performance on one has a correlating effect on others. Source concentration varies dramatically by platform. In the UK, AI Mode's ten leading source domains accounted for between 23.2% and 35.8% of citations among its 10,000 most-cited UK domains across the seven months, compared with only 12.8% to 15.4% for ChatGPT. Category matters as much as platform. The report finds meaningful differences between sectors including Real Estate, Finance, Industrial and Sports, requiring brands to benchmark themselves against the competitors and source ecosystem relevant to their own market and category rather than relying on a single global AI visibility benchmark. Availability The latest 2026 AI Visibility Index: Where the Top Brands Stand in the UK and US is available at https://ai-visibility-index.semrush.com/downloads/ai-visibility-index-2026-study-h2.

articles.summary: Firing a 12 gauge from a frozen layout blind and firing the same gun on a warm September evening hits your ears differently. The frozen ground and open water reflects sound instead of absorbing it, making the impulse noise louder. And if you’re wearing cold protection clothing like a hood, face mask, and thick gloves, you’d have a tougher time working the small dial on your hearing protection device. Cold weather is also the season when your hearing protection gear can start to fail: batteries lose power faster, foam and silicone tips stiffen, and condensation builds inside muff cups when you move from a heated truck into a blind. That’s something you won’t find on a hearing protection spec sheet until legal shooting light, and by then there’s no time left to fix it. Quick answer: Hunt Best Fit Why Waterfowl blind, hooded and layered Electronic earbuds Seal stays intact under a hood or beanie Late season stand, predator calling Electronic earmuffs Warmer, bigger battery, easier controls with gloves Any open-country hunt Add a wind filter Cuts wind roar before amplification picks it up Hunting with a dog Keep the dog off the muzzle line Dogs take the shot's impulse with no protection at all Do Hunters Need Ear Protection in Cold Weather? Yes, even more so than in warm weather. The NIOSH-defined risk of noise-induced hearing loss applies at any temperature, but cold weather adds complications on top of it. Dense, frozen air carries gunfire farther, and the gear built to protect your hearing is more likely to fail. Waterfowlers face higher noise impulses through close-range shooting with two or three guns firing within seconds of each other. Hoods and beanies sit on your head where an earmuff needs a clean seal against the skull. All these factors combine and put the ears of cold season hunters at a higher risk. How Freezing Temperatures Break Down Hearing Protection There are four ways that freezing temperatures can make your hearing protection fail. Each one can be easy to miss until it happens in the field. Cold Drains Lithium Batteries Fast A lithium battery delivering full capacity at 80°F can deliver just half that at 0°F. Even when your device is fully charged in your heated truck, it can still run out of juice before the hunt ends. Tip: Charge your devices fully the night before your hunt and carry spares in an inside jacket pocket against your body heat. Moving From Warm to Cold Can Create Condensation Moving gear from a heated truck cab into freezing air does what a cold drink does on a summer day: moisture condenses on and inside it. This can corrode contacts throughout the cold weather hunting season. Tip: Give your gear a few minutes to acclimate in an unheated space instead of carrying it straight from heater vents into 20°F air. Freezing Air Stiffens Foam and Silicone Tips A silicone tip that seals your ears well at 60°F can stop compressing properly at 20°F, letting sound leak around the seal. Tip: Warm the tips in a pocket before putting them in your ears, and recheck the seal after any adjustment to your hood or mask. Heavy Gloves Defeat Small Controls Small buttons and touch controls on compact earbuds are difficult to operate with heavy gloves on, and numb fingers just make it worse. Tip: Set the volume, mode, and Bluetooth pairing on your ear protection devices before your hands get cold. Running through those four potential issues the night before a hunt can be the difference between gear that works and gear that fails without warning. But what’s the better choice between earbuds or earmuffs when it comes to cold season hunting? Why Earbuds Beat Earmuffs Under a Hood or Beanie In-ear electronic protection beats electronic earmuffs under a hood, beanie, or face mask for one mechanical reason: earbuds sit inside the ear canal, so thick headwear has nothing to lift off or compress against, while a muff cup relies on a seal that a hood or beanie can break. Why a Hood or Beanie Breaks a Muff's Seal An earmuff needs full, even contact around the ear. A beanie or insulated hood pulled up against the cold sits in that exact spot that your earmuff needs to be. Earbuds skip this problem and stay clear of a shotgun's stock during repeated cheek welds. Factor Electronic Earbuds Electronic Earmuffs Seal under a hood or beanie Stays sealed inside the ear canal Hood or beanie lifts the cup and breaks the seal Warmth No warmth benefit on its own Cups add real warmth over the ears Control access with gloves Small buttons or touch controls, best preset before hands go cold Larger dials, easier to adjust with gloves on Cold weather battery runtime Smaller battery, more exposed to ambient cold Larger battery reserve, typically holds a charge longer in the cold Cheek weld or gun mount No interference with the stock Cup can lift or lose contact during repeated mounting Best for Waterfowl blinds and any hooded, layered, mobile hunt Static stand sits, predator calling, or anyone prioritizing warmth Warmth and Bigger Controls: Where Muffs Beat Earbuds Earbuds may have the seal advantage, but it doesn’t make them the right choice every time. Muffs run warmer, hold larger batteries, and use bigger dials that are easier to find with gloves on. That’s what makes them the better choice for stand hunting and static predator calling. If you’re shooting at close range with other blind mates, the combined muzzle blast can exceed a single earbud's protection ceiling. Check our doubling up with plugs and muffs guide for how to pair a passive plug underneath ear muffs. Solving the seal problem still doesn’t fix the loudest complaint waterfowlers have: what wind does to sound amplification. Why Amplified Hearing Protection Struggles in Open Wind With amplified hearing protection, the same microphone and gain that boosts a wingbeat or a call also boosts moving air. In an open marsh, a light breeze can turn into a roar loud enough to mask the sounds any hunter is trying to hear. A microphone doesn’t know the difference between a wingbeat and moving air across its port. Turn the gain up enough to catch a hen mallard at fifty yards, and a fifteen mile per hour wind gets amplified right along with it. That’s a problem most gear testing never catches because they test at a range, not in a blind facing open water. Here’s two adjustments to fix the problem: reducing gain slightly instead of running it maxed out, and blocking wind before it reaches the microphone. AXIL's GSX foam wind filter, built for the GS Extreme earbud line, fits over the microphone port and breaks up airflow before it hits the mic. Facing a blind opening away from the wind can cut wind load before any filter or gain adjustment even comes into play. Hearing Calls, Wings, and Shots: The Waterfowl Ear Protection Problem A duck blind demands hearing protection that lets a hunter catch a call, a wingbeat, and a shot call. Sometimes you need to hear all three inside a few seconds, while still surviving water, cold, and multiple guns firing at once. That’s why most experienced waterfowlers reject passive plugs outright and run electronic protection instead. Foam or silicone plugs block sound in both directions. They protect against the shot, but they also block the exact sounds a duck hunter is listening for: the low whistle of wings cupping toward the decoys, a call from a hunting partner, or the moment someone says take them. Electronic earbuds solve that by amplifying ambient sound up to the moment a shot fires, then cutting the signal within milliseconds to block the gunshot's impulse. AXIL's XCOR PRO earbuds, for example, compress incoming sound once it crosses 85 decibels, the same threshold NIOSH flag as risky sustained exposure, while carrying an NRR of 21 to 23 depending on tip size. A duck blind at first light is also one of the loudest recreational shooting environments there is, since two or three guns often fire within a second of a flock working the decoys. Treat NRR as a starting point and consider doubling up with a passive plug on the loudest mornings. Rifle vs Shotgun: How Exposure Changes Your Ear Protection Priorities A shotgun fires multiple close-range shots in quick succession, so waterfowl hunters lean on amplification and a fast cutoff. A rifle produces one sharper impulse at typically longer range, which puts more weight on peak NRR and a seal that holds through hours in a stand. A late season deer hunter sitting a stand for hours can keep their hands stuffed in a pocket instead of working their gear. That warmth is crucial when you need to keep a low profile, and makes electronic earmuffs the best choice for a static cold sit. Winter predator calling adds another hunting advantage: a coyote approaching from downwind gives itself away through the same faint sounds that are amplified by electronic hearing protection. The same cold weather mechanics still apply regardless of your choice of firearms, with batteries draining faster in a 15°F stand than on a 60°F afternoon. Every hunter in a duck blind or a deer stand protects their own ears. But a hunting dog sits closer to the muzzle than anyone else in the blind, and gets no hearing protection at all. Don't Forget the Dog: What Gunfire Does to a Retriever's Hearing A retriever positioned in a duck blind sits closer to the muzzle than any human hunter and takes the full, unprotected impulse of every shot fired. Several published studies link this to measurable hearing loss in working gun dogs. A practical tip is to position your dogs as far from the muzzle as the blind allows, avoid shots taken directly over its head when a safer angle exists, and consider a canine-specific hearing protection product for dogs that hunt dozens of days a season. Cold Weather Ear Protection Checklist Running through a short checklist the night before a cold-weather hunt catches most of the hearing protection gear failures before they can happen in the field. Stage Action Night before Charge earbuds or muffs fully, pack spare batteries, warm and inspect foam or silicone tips for stiffness, preset volume and Bluetooth pairing In the truck Let gear acclimate to outside temperature for a few minutes rather than carrying it straight from heater vents into freezing air In the blind or stand Keep spare batteries in an inside pocket against body heat, fit the wind filter before shooting light, recheck the seal every time a hood or face mask gets adjusted After the hunt Dry earbuds or muffs thoroughly before storing them, since leftover moisture from condensation is what damages electronics over a season Frequently Asked Questions on Cold Weather Ear Protection Do hunters wear ear protection? Historically, most do not. Roughly 70 to 80 percent of hunters report never wearing hearing protection while hunting and hunters as a group show measurably higher rates of hearing loss as a result. Does cold weather damage electronic ear protection? Not on its own. Cold reduces battery runtime temporarily and raises the risk of condensation when gear moves quickly between a heated space and freezing air. Acclimating gear gradually and drying it fully after use prevents the moisture-related damage that shortens a device's life. Will earmuffs fit under a hunting hood or beanie? Usually poorly. A hood, beanie, or face mask sits in the exact spot an earmuff needs to seal against the skull, and headwear thick enough for a cold morning typically lifts the cup and breaks that seal. That is the main reason in-ear protection is the better choice for hooded, layered hunts. Can a hunter wear ear protection and still hear duck calls? Yes. Electronic hearing protection amplifies ambient sound, including calls and wingbeats, up to the moment a shot fires, so a hunter running it typically hears better than a hunter wearing no protection at all. How long do batteries last in freezing temperatures? Expect noticeably less than the rated runtime. Lithium batteries can drop to roughly half their normal capacity at 0°F, though the exact loss depends on the device and the temperature. Charge fully the night before, carry a spare against body heat, and test a specific setup cold before relying on it for a full morning. Do hunting dogs need ear protection? The research is limited but consistent: dogs that hunt regularly near gunfire measure worse on hearing tests than dogs that do not. Simple, low-cost mitigations follow regardless of any formal recommendation, such as positioning a dog away from the muzzle and avoiding shots taken directly over its head. Match the Gear to the Hunt If you’re looking forward to a good hunting season, don’t forget to pay attention to your hearing protection gear. A pair of earbuds that seal well on the couch can behave differently after thirty minutes in a truck bed at 15°F. The week before opening morning is the best time to find that out, not first light on opening day. Set the volume and mode, leave the gear in an unheated garage or a cooler outside for the length of an actual sit, and confirm that the seal, the controls, and the runtime hold up before opening morning. Shop AXIL's shooting and hunting hearing protection collection ahead of the opener, and give whatever setup you picked a real cold-weather test before it has to work for real.
